In 2011, researchers confirmed the pathogen: *Yersinia pestis*. In 2022, a team from the Max Planck Institute traced its origin to Central Asia, near Lake Issyk-Kul in present-day Kyrgyzstan. Tombstones from 1338–1339 record "pestilence." DNA extracted from three bodies confirmed plague bacteria.

The transmission mechanism is still debated. The mainstream view: rat fleas spread bubonic plague. But the Black Death moved faster than rat-flea transmission alone can explain. Human fleas and lice may have played a role. Scientists are still working on it.

But people in 1348 could only see what the disease did. Swellings in the groin and armpits. Black spots spreading across the skin. Death.

---

[CH05 | 8:36-10:17 | arrival_mechanism]

The plague spread along existing networks. Markets met once a week. Mills ground grain for multiple households. Churches held Sunday services. Manor courts settled disputes. People traveled short distances constantly. To the next village. To the nearest town.

Some cities tried to stop it. They closed gates. They banned travelers from infected areas.

It didn't work.

The disease had already entered before the gates closed. Merchants kept moving. Pilgrims kept traveling. Armies marched. Rats and fleas ignored human borders.

Boccaccio put it simply: the plague came "like any other goods, by the roads."

So the plague reached villages the same way everything else did. By road.

---

[CH06 | 10:17-12:05 | stakes_immersion]

A typical peasant house: timber frame, wattle-and-daub walls, thatched roof. Grain stored indoors in sacks or barrels.

Warm. Dark. Food everywhere. The structure was comfortable for rats and fleas too.

When the plague arrived, this is what people saw.

Boccaccio described it: swellings the size of eggs or apples appeared in the groin or armpit. Then black spots spread across the body. Those spots were a death sentence.

He also recorded this: he saw two pigs rooting through rags discarded by a plague victim. The pigs staggered, collapsed, and died shortly after.

There were three forms of plague. Bubonic plague — transmitted by flea bites — caused swollen lymph nodes and killed 50 to 60 percent of victims without treatment. Pneumonic plague — airborne, human-to-human — caused coughing and bloody sputum. It killed nearly everyone within three days. Septicemic plague — bacteria directly in the bloodstream — could kill within 24 hours.

---

[CH07 | 12:05-13:45 | care_system]

Manorial records show no payments to physicians. Hospitals, where they existed, served cities and monasteries. Physicians were rare and expensive. Ordinary villagers could not afford them.

Care fell to families and neighbors.

A new occupation emerged: *becchini*, professional corpse collectors. They came from the poorest layers of society and were paid to haul bodies on carts or stretchers.

Guy de Chauliac, the pope's physician, recommended burning fires day and night in the sickroom, refusing visitors, and avoiding bad air. Pope Clement VI followed the advice and survived.

The measures helped. Fire and isolation reduced exposure to airborne and contact transmission. But they could not stop flea-borne spread.

The pope also took other steps. He consecrated the entire Rhône River as a burial site when graveyards ran out of space. He declared that anyone who died of plague would be absolved of sin, since there was no time for last rites. In 1348 alone, he lost six cardinals.

Priests went house to house to administer last rites: confession, communion, anointing. They had to enter the rooms where the sick were dying. They had to touch them.

That made clergy the most exposed group.

---

[CH08 | 13:45-15:42 | institutional_strain]

Bishops' registers show the toll. Approximately four out of every ten parish clergy with a benefice died during the epidemic. Some parishes replaced the priest twice in a single year.

The system bent under pressure.

Ralph of Shrewsbury, Bishop of Bath and Wells, issued a written document around 1348. It stated: a person facing death without access to a priest could confess to a layperson. If no man was available, even to a woman.

This is the most astonishing document in the entire story.

It is a written adjustment to the most important sacrament in medieval Christianity. It shows how far the institution had to bend to keep functioning.

---

[CH09 | 15:42-18:33 | dignity_reveal]

Normally, the dead were buried in the churchyard. A priest presided. The family attended.

When death rates spiked, the system strained. Pope Clement consecrated the Rhône River as burial space. Venice established a health board in 1348 to regulate corpse transport and mandate grave depth.

Archaeologists excavated a mass grave in East Smithfield, London — used between 1348 and 1350. It held 48 bodies. More than half were children. But they were still laid out head-to-foot in organized rows.

What struck researchers was not chaos. It was order.

Even under extreme pressure, the people who buried them tried to maintain dignity.

Boccaccio described people fleeing, abandoning the sick. But archaeology and records show that most people stayed. They cared for the sick. They buried the dead. They kept the system running.

The clearest example: Eyam, a village in Derbyshire. In 1665, plague arrived in a cloth shipment from London. The tailor who received it, George Viccars, died within a week. By September, six were dead. By October, 23.

The rector, William Mompesson, and the Puritan minister Thomas Stanley convinced the village to seal itself off. No one would leave for 14 months.

They moved church services outdoors to a valley called Cucklett Delph. Families buried their own dead. Neighboring villages left food and medicine at boundary stones. Villagers paid with coins soaked in vinegar.

Elizabeth Hancock buried her husband and six children in eight days in August 1666. She survived. Marshall Howe, the gravedigger, handled countless bodies and never got sick.

273 people died — about 260 recorded deaths out of a population estimated between 350 and 800. Roughly one in four survived.

The plague stayed contained. It did not spread to surrounding villages.

The village has held a memorial service every August since 1866.

So before we go further: if you want to see how this story ends, subscribe now. The most surprising part happens after the dying stops.

---

[CH10 | 18:33-21:35 | death_accounting]

Now: how do we know how many people died?

Because of heriot.

When a tenant died, the manor court recorded the payment. One ox. One cow. Sometimes cash. Every death generated a record.

Historians studying these court rolls have calculated mortality rates village by village.

Halesowen manor: 40 to 43 percent of tenants died. Winchester episcopal estates: close to 50 percent. Cottenham in Cambridgeshire: 49 percent.

The most shocking case: an Essex manor where all twelve principal tenant farmers — peasants who held standard family farms — died in 1349. In a single season.

These were not marginal figures. They were the backbone of the village. They plowed the most land. They owed the most labor. They testified in court. They organized the harvest.

Now their names stopped appearing in the records.

Overall, England lost between one-third and one-half of its population. Some areas lost 60 percent. But the variation was enormous. Some villages lost only 10 to 20 percent. Others nearly vanished.

---

[CH11 | 21:35-23:13 | aftermath_tableau]

Harvest season does not wait. Neither does planting season.

Agnolo di Tura, a chronicler in Siena, wrote: "I buried my five children with my own hands. Many said and believed: this is the end of the world."

English chronicles recorded: "Fields went unharvested. Houses stood empty."

Fields. Houses. Villages. Mills.

The land did not change. But the people who worked it were gone.

Before, a peasant might wait his entire life to inherit his father's land. Now he could choose between multiple manors.

Neighboring lords were competing for labor. They offered lower rents. Fewer labor obligations.

Economic historian Thorold Rogers calculated that real wages in 15th-century England were about double what they had been before 1346. That level was not reached again until the 1880s or 1890s — roughly 500 years later.

---

[CH12 | 23:13-25:39 | consequence_chain]

Survivors realized they had bargaining power.

Lords needed labor. Survivors could walk to the next village and negotiate better terms.

The government tried to suppress it. In 1349, Parliament passed the Ordinance of Labourers. In 1351, the Statute of Labourers. Both laws attempted to freeze wages at 1346 levels and prohibit workers from moving freely.

Basic arithmetic could not be overridden. There were far fewer people, but just as much land.

Wages rose anyway, through the cracks in enforcement.

Over the next decades, the system transformed. Rent payments shifted from labor to cash. Inheritance rules loosened — younger sons and daughters could inherit, not just the eldest son. Serfdom effectively disappeared by around 1400.

The long-term evidence: the Peasants' Revolt of 1381. Tens of thousands marched on London demanding the abolition of serfdom and lower rents.

---

[CH13 | 25:39-26:50 | myth_correction]

Popular belief holds that the Black Death wiped out entire villages overnight.

There is evidence for it. Between 1350 and 1500, more than 1,300 English villages were abandoned.

The reality is more complicated.

Large-scale studies of deserted villages show that most were abandoned in the 15th century due to the wool economy and enclosure, not the Black Death.

Instant destruction was rare. Prolonged decline was common.

---

[CH14 | 26:50-28:41 | survivor_voice]

Direct testimony from ordinary people is rare.

But there is one.

In the church tower of St. Mary's, Ashwell, Hertfordshire, someone carved an inscription around 1350. In Latin: "1349. The plague was fierce and violent. Only the poor remain to witness."

We do not know who wrote it.

An anonymous witness carved a warning for future generations.

The plague did not end in 1349.

It returned in 1361–62. Then 1369. Then 1375. Then the 1390s. Then the 1400s. It came back every five to twelve years for nearly 400 years.

The second wave in 1361–62 showed different selectivity. English nobles died at about 23 percent — lower than the first wave. But children and teenagers died at higher rates. Survivors of the first wave had some immunity. Children born after 1348 had none.

Europe's population did not recover to 1348 levels until the 16th century — roughly 200 years later.

---

[CH15 | 28:41-30:49 | legacy_bridge]

So why was it so deadly?

Part of the answer: no germ theory. People did not know bacteria existed until the 1860s. No antibiotics — those were not invented until the 1940s. High population density. Malnutrition. Three forms of plague attacking at once.

There is also evidence of biological selection. A 2022 *Nature* study analyzed 206 ancient DNA samples. It found that people carrying two copies of a protective variant near the ERAP2 gene had roughly 40 percent higher survival rates during the Black Death.

The cost: that same variant is a risk factor for Crohn's disease and other autoimmune disorders today.

The plague also left institutional legacies. On July 27, 1377, the port republic of Ragusa — now Dubrovnik, Croatia — passed a law requiring travelers from plague zones to isolate for 30 days, later extended to 40. The English word "quarantine" comes from the Italian *quarantina* — forty days. In 1423, Venice established the world's first quarantine island, Lazzaretto Vecchio.

The plague returned in 1665 in London — about 100,000 dead. In 1720 in Marseille — another 100,000.

Today, antibiotics can treat plague if caught early. But it has not disappeared. According to the World Health Organization, there are still several hundred to several thousand cases globally each year, mainly in Africa, Asia, and the Americas.

One more thing. In 1348, there were no plague doctors in bird masks. That costume was invented in 1619. The nursery rhyme "Ring Around the Rosie" is not about the Black Death — that is a later myth. The claim that Jews were immune or poisoned wells? Pope Clement VI pointed out at the time that Jews were dying in large numbers too. Between 1348 and 1351, about 350 anti-Jewish massacres occurred, 60 large communities and 150 small ones were destroyed.

---

[CH16 | 30:49-33:05 | closure]

So: when the Black Death reached an English village, what happened?

How did it arrive? Along trade routes and everyday networks. Markets. Mills. Churches. Courts. It came the same way everything else came.

How many died? Between one-third and one-half. In some places, 60 percent. In one Essex manor, all twelve principal tenant farmers died in the same season.

Why was it so deadly? No knowledge of bacteria. No antibiotics. Malnutrition. Genetic variation. Three forms of plague at once. How exactly it spread — rat fleas, human lice, or both — remains debated.

What changed? Labor became scarce. Wages doubled. Serfdom collapsed. Parliament tried to freeze wages. Basic arithmetic defeated the law. Rent shifted from labor to cash. Inheritance rules loosened. In 1381, tens of thousands of peasants marched on London.

The village did not end. In most places, it continued.

Someone plowed the field. Someone rang the church bell. Someone recorded the heriot payment in the court roll.

Forests began to recover in some regions — pollen data from 2022 shows that farmland reverted to woodland in England, northern France, and northern Italy, though Ireland and parts of Eastern Europe were less affected.

At Eyam, survivors kept living. The village has held a memorial service every year since 1866. The author of the Ashwell inscription is lost to history.

The plague came back every five to twelve years for nearly 400 years. It did not truly end until the age of antibiotics. Even today, the World Health Organization records hundreds to thousands of cases annually.

The most amazing thing is not the death toll. It is that they continued.

We think of plague as distant history. But it returned for four centuries. Only antibiotics made it truly treatable.

Chronicled at the scale of kingdoms and continents. Lived at the scale of cottages and fields.

final_script:
# Optimized Script

[CH01 | 0:00-1:37 | scene_entry]

October 1347. Messina, a port in southern Italy.

Twelve Genoese galleys limp into harbor. The sailors are sick. Some are already dead. Others are dying.

A notary and chronicler, Gabriele de' Mussis, records what he sees. He writes that the ships brought cargo — and something else.

That something else is plague.

Within months, it spreads north through Italy. By June 1348, it crosses into France. By summer, it reaches the English coast. A merchant ship from Brittany docks at Melcombe, Dorset. The disease comes ashore.

In two years, plague travels from Caffa on the Black Sea — where Mongol forces besieging the city reportedly catapulted infected corpses over the walls — to the English countryside. More than 2,000 miles. Following trade routes. Following roads. Following rivers. Following people.

This is not the story of one exceptional village. This is the kind of village most people actually lived in.

England in 1348 has between 8,000 and 9,000 villages and manors — estimates based on Domesday Book projections and manorial records. The population is around five to six million, according to demographic historians who reconstructed it from tax records and parish registers. About 90 percent live in agricultural communities. The same baptismal font. The same weddings. The same graveyard. The same fields.

When the plague arrives in England, it arrives in places like this.

---

[CH02 | 1:37-2:50 | premise_hook]

What happened next is documented history, not folklore.

The evidence: manorial court rolls listing deaths, land transfers, heriot payments. Bishops' registers tracking clergy deaths and replacements. Chronicles written by people who were there. Archaeology. Parish records.

In 2011, scientists at McMaster University and the University of Tübingen extracted DNA from teeth of plague victims buried in East Smithfield, London. They reconstructed the full genome of *Yersinia pestis*, the bacterium that caused the Black Death. That strain is the ancestor of every plague strain on earth today.

Because these records survive, what happened next is not speculation or legend. It is history we can count, trace, and verify.

So: when the Black Death reached an English village, what actually happened?

Who had a chance to survive? How did people respond? What determined who lived and who died? What did the world look like afterward?

---

[CH03 | 2:50-5:34 | world_before_context]

Before the plague, England is crowded. The population has reached five to six million. Arable land has been pushed to its limit. Nearly every acre that can be plowed is already under cultivation.

The country has already been through trauma. Between 1315 and 1322, a great famine kills hundreds of thousands. Harvests fail. Grain prices spike. People starve. In 1319, a cattle plague wipes out livestock across the country. Oxen die. Plows sit idle.

By 1348, the country has recovered somewhat. But the memory is still fresh.

Most people live under the manorial system. The basic unit: a manor. The lord owns the land. Peasants — tenants — farm plots in exchange for labor. A tenant might owe three days a week to plow the lord's fields, haul grain, repair fences. The rest of the week, he works his own plot. Rent comes as labor, not cash.

The manor court meets regularly. It records disputes. Land transfers. Marriages. Deaths.

And when a tenant dies, the family owes the lord a heriot. The best ox. The best cow. The best horse. Sometimes cash instead. It is a death tax. It is also an inheritance fee — proof that the family can take over the land.

The pope also took other steps. He consecrated the entire Rhône River as a burial site when graveyards ran out of space. He declared that anyone who died of plague would be absolved of sin, since there was no time for last rites. In 1348 alone, he lost six cardinals.

Priests went house to house to administer last rites: confession, communion, anointing. They had to enter the rooms where the sick were dying. They had to touch them.

That made clergy the most exposed group.

---

[CH08 | 13:45-15:42 | institutional_strain]

Bishops' registers show the toll. Approximately four out of every ten parish clergy with a benefice died during the epidemic. Some parishes replaced the priest twice in a single year.

The system bent under pressure.

Ralph of Shrewsbury, Bishop of Bath and Wells, issued a written document around 1348. It stated: a person facing death without access to a priest could confess to a layperson. If no man was available, even to a woman.

This is the most astonishing document in the entire story.

It is a written adjustment to the most important sacrament in medieval Christianity. It shows how far the institution had to bend to keep functioning.

---

[CH09 | 15:42-18:33 | dignity_reveal]

Normally, the dead were buried in the churchyard. A priest presided. The family attended.

When death rates spiked, the system strained. Pope Clement consecrated the Rhône River as burial space. Venice established a health board in 1348 to regulate corpse transport and mandate grave depth.

Archaeologists excavated a mass grave in East Smithfield, London — used between 1348 and 1350. It held 48 bodies. More than half were children. But they were still laid out head-to-foot in organized rows.

What struck researchers was not chaos. It was order.

Even under extreme pressure, the people who buried them tried to maintain dignity.

Boccaccio described people fleeing, abandoning the sick. But archaeology and records show that most people stayed. They cared for the sick. They buried the dead. They kept the system running.

The clearest example: Eyam, a village in Derbyshire. In 1665, plague arrived in a cloth shipment from London. The tailor who received it, George Viccars, died within a week. By September, six were dead. By October, 23.

The rector, William Mompesson, and the Puritan minister Thomas Stanley convinced the village to seal itself off. No one would leave for 14 months.

They moved church services outdoors to a valley called Cucklett Delph. Families buried their own dead. Neighboring villages left food and medicine at boundary stones. Villagers paid with coins soaked in vinegar.

Elizabeth Hancock buried her husband and six children in eight days in August 1666. She survived. Marshall Howe, the gravedigger, handled countless bodies and never got sick.

273 people died — about 260 recorded deaths out of a population estimated between 350 and 800. Roughly one in four survived.

The plague stayed contained. It did not spread to surrounding villages.

The village has held a memorial service every August since 1866.

So before we go further: if you want to see how this story ends, subscribe now. The most surprising part happens after the dying stops.

---

[CH10 | 18:33-21:35 | death_accounting]

Now: how do we know how many people died?

Because of heriot.

When a tenant died, the manor court recorded the payment. One ox. One cow. Sometimes cash. Every death generated a record.

Historians studying these court rolls have calculated mortality rates village by village.

Halesowen manor: 40 to 43 percent of tenants died. Winchester episcopal estates: close to 50 percent. Cottenham in Cambridgeshire: 49 percent.

The most shocking case: an Essex manor where all twelve principal tenant farmers — peasants who held standard family farms — died in 1349. In a single season.

These were not marginal figures. They were the backbone of the village. They plowed the most land. They owed the most labor. They testified in court. They organized the harvest.

Now their names stopped appearing in the records.

Overall, England lost between one-third and one-half of its population. Some areas lost 60 percent. But the variation was enormous. Some villages lost only 10 to 20 percent. Others nearly vanished.

---

[CH11 | 21:35-23:13 | aftermath_tableau]

Harvest season does not wait. Neither does planting season.

Agnolo di Tura, a chronicler in Siena, wrote: "I buried my five children with my own hands. Many said and believed: this is the end of the world."

English chronicles recorded: "Fields went unharvested. Houses stood empty."

Fields. Houses. Villages. Mills.

The land did not change. But the people who worked it were gone.

Before, a peasant might wait his entire life to inherit his father's land. Now he could choose between multiple manors.

Neighboring lords were competing for labor. They offered lower rents. Fewer labor obligations.

Economic historian Thorold Rogers calculated that real wages in 15th-century England were about double what they had been before 1346. That level was not reached again until the 1880s or 1890s — roughly 500 years later.

---

[CH12 | 23:13-25:39 | consequence_chain]

Survivors realized they had bargaining power.

Lords needed labor. Survivors could walk to the next village and negotiate better terms.

The government tried to suppress it. In 1349, Parliament passed the Ordinance of Labourers. In 1351, the Statute of Labourers. Both laws attempted to freeze wages at 1346 levels and prohibit workers from moving freely.

Basic arithmetic could not be overridden. There were far fewer people, but just as much land.

Wages rose anyway, through the cracks in enforcement.

Over the next decades, the system transformed. Rent payments shifted from labor to cash. Inheritance rules loosened — younger sons and daughters could inherit, not just the eldest son. Serfdom effectively disappeared by around 1400.

The long-term evidence: the Peasants' Revolt of 1381. Tens of thousands marched on London demanding the abolition of serfdom and lower rents.

---

[CH13 | 25:39-26:50 | myth_correction]

Popular belief holds that the Black Death wiped out entire villages overnight.

There is evidence for it. Between 1350 and 1500, more than 1,300 English villages were abandoned.

The reality is more complicated.

Large-scale studies of deserted villages show that most were abandoned in the 15th century due to the wool economy and enclosure, not the Black Death.

Instant destruction was rare. Prolonged decline was common.

---

[CH14 | 26:50-28:41 | survivor_voice]

Direct testimony from ordinary people is rare.

But there is one.

In the church tower of St. Mary's, Ashwell, Hertfordshire, someone carved an inscription around 1350. In Latin: "1349. The plague was fierce and violent. Only the poor remain to witness."

We do not know who wrote it.

An anonymous witness carved a warning for future generations.

The plague did not end in 1349.

It returned in 1361–62. Then 1369. Then 1375. Then the 1390s. Then the 1400s. It came back every five to twelve years for nearly 400 years.

The second wave in 1361–62 showed different selectivity. English nobles died at about 23 percent — lower than the first wave. But children and teenagers died at higher rates. Survivors of the first wave had some immunity. Children born after 1348 had none.

Europe's population did not recover to 1348 levels until the 16th century — roughly 200 years later.

---

[CH15 | 28:41-30:49 | legacy_bridge]

So why was it so deadly?

Part of the answer: no germ theory. People did not know bacteria existed until the 1860s. No antibiotics — those were not invented until the 1940s. High population density. Malnutrition. Three forms of plague attacking at once.

There is also evidence of biological selection. A 2022 *Nature* study analyzed 206 ancient DNA samples. It found that people carrying two copies of a protective variant near the ERAP2 gene had roughly 40 percent higher survival rates during the Black Death.

The cost: that same variant is a risk factor for Crohn's disease and other autoimmune disorders today.

The plague also left institutional legacies. On July 27, 1377, the port republic of Ragusa — now Dubrovnik, Croatia — passed a law requiring travelers from plague zones to isolate for 30 days, later extended to 40. The English word "quarantine" comes from the Italian *quarantina* — forty days. In 1423, Venice established the world's first quarantine island, Lazzaretto Vecchio.

The plague returned in 1665 in London — about 100,000 dead. In 1720 in Marseille — another 100,000.

Today, antibiotics can treat plague if caught early. But it has not disappeared. According to the World Health Organization, there are still several hundred to several thousand cases globally each year, mainly in Africa, Asia, and the Americas.

One more thing. In 1348, there were no plague doctors in bird masks. That costume was invented in 1619. The nursery rhyme "Ring Around the Rosie" is not about the Black Death — that is a later myth. The claim that Jews were immune or poisoned wells? Pope Clement VI pointed out at the time that Jews were dying in large numbers too. Between 1348 and 1351, about 350 anti-Jewish massacres occurred, 60 large communities and 150 small ones were destroyed.

---

[CH16 | 30:49-33:05 | closure]

So: when the Black Death reached an English village, what happened?

How did it arrive? Along trade routes and everyday networks. Markets. Mills. Churches. Courts. It came the same way everything else came.

How many died? Between one-third and one-half. In some places, 60 percent. In one Essex manor, all twelve principal tenant farmers died in the same season.

Why was it so deadly? No knowledge of bacteria. No antibiotics. Malnutrition. Genetic variation. Three forms of plague at once. How exactly it spread — rat fleas, human lice, or both — remains debated.

What changed? Labor became scarce. Wages doubled. Serfdom collapsed. Parliament tried to freeze wages. Basic arithmetic defeated the law. Rent shifted from labor to cash. Inheritance rules loosened. In 1381, tens of thousands of peasants marched on London.

The village did not end. In most places, it continued.

Someone plowed the field. Someone rang the church bell. Someone recorded the heriot payment in the court roll.

Forests began to recover in some regions — pollen data from 2022 shows that farmland reverted to woodland in England, northern France, and northern Italy, though Ireland and parts of Eastern Europe were less affected.

At Eyam, survivors kept living. The village has held a memorial service every year since 1866. The author of the Ashwell inscription is lost to history.

The plague came back every five to twelve years for nearly 400 years. It did not truly end until the age of antibiotics. Even today, the World Health Organization records hundreds to thousands of cases annually.

The most amazing thing is not the death toll. It is that they continued.

We think of plague as distant history. But it returned for four centuries. Only antibiotics made it truly treatable.

Chronicled at the scale of kingdoms and continents. Lived at the scale of cottages and fields.

stale_facts.content: 1348年6月，意大利南部港口墨西拿(Messina)，12艘热那亚桨帆船载着病死的船员驶入港口。编年史家的记录：水手带来'别的东西'。
1348年6月，英格兰多塞特郡梅尔库姆港(Melcombe)，货船从法国布列塔尼抵达，疫情从此登陆英格兰。
黑死病从1346年黑海卡法(Caffa)传至1348年英格兰，沿商路蔓延两年，覆盖从中亚、地中海到西欧的地理范围。
这不是某一个村，而是大多数人真实生活的那种村：同一个洗礼池、同一场婚礼、同一片墓地。英格兰有约8000-9000个村庄与庄园，绝大多数人口生活在这样的农业社区。
证据来源包括：(1)庄园法庭卷宗(manorial court rolls)记录佃户死亡与土地继承；(2)主教登记册记录神职人员死亡与岗位更替；(3)编年史家亲历记录(薄伽丘《十日谈》、迪·图拉、德·肖利亚克)；(4)考古证据(伦敦东史密斯菲尔德瘟疫墓地、从死者牙齿提取DNA)；(5)教堂登记簿(伊姆村273名死者姓名)。
2011年《自然》(Nature)期刊：加拿大麦克马斯特大学与德国图宾根大学团队从伦敦东史密斯菲尔德瘟疫墓地(1348-1350年启用)死者的牙齿中提取DNA，重建了黑死病病原体的完整基因组，证明病原体为鼠疫耶尔森菌(Yersinia pestis)，且该菌株是今天全球所有鼠疫菌株的祖先。
1348年前英格兰人口约500-600万，可耕地已达极限。1315-1322年大饥荒、1319年牲畜大疫已造成创伤。
农民依附于庄园(manor)，以劳役(labor service)换取土地耕作权。领主拥有土地，佃户(tenant)耕种并缴纳地租与劳役。
葬礼税(heriot)：佃户死亡时，家人需向领主缴纳最好的牲畜或现金作为'死亡税'。这一琐碎的税收制度让今天的历史学家能够从庄园法庭卷宗中精确统计死亡人数与时间——因为每一笔heriot都被逐一记录在案。
临终圣礼(last rites)包括告解(confession)、圣餐(communion)、临终涂油(extreme unction)。中世纪信仰认为灵魂重于身体，未经临终圣礼而死意味着灵魂无法进入天堂。神父必须挨家挨户执行这些仪式。
巴黎大学医学院1348年解释：星象不吉(土星、木星、火星合相)导致瘴气(miasma)——腐败空气传播疾病。教会解释：神对人类罪恶的惩罚。两套解释在当时并行不悖。
2011年《自然》：从600多年前受害者遗骸中重建鼠疫耶尔森菌基因组，确认病原体。2022年《自然》：德国马克斯·普朗克研究所在吉尔吉斯斯坦伊塞克湖附近墓地(1338-1339年)找到关键证据，墓碑铭文写'瘟疫'，7具遗骸中3具检出鼠疫菌DNA，锁定起源地在中亚天山一带。
传播机制在科学界仍有争议：主流认为是鼠-蚤传播(腺鼠疫)，但黑死病传播速度远超单纯鼠蚤模型能解释的范围，人蚤/人虱是否参与传播至今是学术争论。
薄伽丘《十日谈》记载：'男男女女最初在腹股沟或腋下生出肿块(gavocciolo)，有的像鸡蛋，有的像苹果……随后全身出现黑斑或瘀斑——这就是死亡的预告。'命名'黑死病'来自皮下出血导致的皮肤发黑(败血型鼠疫)。
三种临床形态：(1)腺鼠疫(bubonic plague)：跳蚤叮咬传播，淋巴结肿大，不治死亡率约50-60%；(2)肺鼠疫(pneumonic plague)：飞沫人际传播，咯血，死亡率几乎100%，三天内致死；(3)败血型鼠疫(septicemic plague)：细菌直接入血，最快24小时内死亡。
村庄与外界的日常连接：集市(market，每周一次)、磨坊(mill，磨面粉)、教堂(church，礼拜日礼拜)、法庭(manorial court，处理纠纷)。这些短途出行织成了传播网络。
部分城市尝试关闭城门、禁止来自疫区的旅客，但拦截失败。原因：(1)疫情已在关门前进入；(2)商人、朝圣者、军队持续流动；(3)鼠类与跳蚤无视人类边界。薄伽丘总结：'像一切货物一样沿公路而来。'
普通家庭居所：木骨泥墙(wattle and daub)、茅草顶(thatched roof)、粮食储存在室内麻袋或木桶中。这样的居所对老鼠与跳蚤'也很舒适'——温暖、黑暗、食物充足。
专业医疗的三重缺位：(1)诊所(clinic)不存在于村庄；(2)医院(hospital)主要服务城市与修道院；(3)医生(physician)极其稀缺且昂贵，普通村民无法负担。民间照护由家庭成员与邻里承担。
德·肖利亚克(Guy de Chauliac，教皇御医)建议：房间内昼夜燃火、谢绝访客、避免瘴气。教皇克雷芒六世照做并活了下来。双向评价：燃火与隔离确实减少了暴露(现代视角：减少了飞沫与接触传播)，但无法阻断鼠蚤传播。
神父挨家挨户执行临终圣礼(告解、圣餐、临终涂油)，必须进入病人房间、近距离接触病人。这使得神职人员成为暴露最多的高危人群。
英格兰神职人员(有圣俸者，beneficed clergy)死亡率约40%。例如：一年内同一教区更替两任神父的记录屡见不鲜。
巴斯与韦尔斯主教拉尔夫(Ralph of Shrewsbury，约1348年)发布书面文件：允许临终者在无神父的情况下向平信徒(layperson)甚至妇女(women)告解。这是对最重要圣礼的书面调整，体现制度在压力下的崩解。
伦敦东史密斯菲尔德瘟疫墓地考古(1348-1350年)：集体墓48人，过半为儿童，但仍按头脚朝向(head-to-foot orientation)整齐安放。反转句：'让研究者震撼的不是混乱，而是体面。'
薄伽丘《十日谈》描述'兄弟抛弃兄弟、父母拒绝照料子女'，但考古与档案显示：绝大多数村庄的人没有逃离，而是留下照顾病人、安葬死者、维持制度。伊姆村(1665-1666年)全村自我隔离14个月，是坚守的教科书案例。
庄园法庭卷宗(manorial court rolls)记录：(1)黑尔索温庄园(Halesowen)：佃户死亡约40-43%；(2)温彻斯特主教庄园：接近50%；(3)剑桥郡科滕纳姆(Cottenham)：49%。最冲击性个案：埃塞克斯某庄园十二户主要佃农(principal tenants)全部死于同一季。
英格兰村庄总体死亡率约1/3至1/2(33%-50%)，重灾区达60%。但地区极不均衡：部分村庄损失轻微(10-20%)，部分接近全灭(70-80%)。
锡耶纳编年史家迪·图拉(Agnolo di Tura)：'父亲不去看儿子，教堂不再敲钟，人们说也相信：这就是世界末日。我亲手埋葬了我的五个孩子。'英格兰编年史：'田地无人收割，房屋空无一人。'
劳动力稀缺导致幸存者议价能力大增。从前一个农民等一辈子才能继承父亲的土地，现在他可以在多个庄园之间挑选条件更好的土地。邻村庄主也在竞争劳动力，提供更低的地租、更少的劳役。
英格兰农业工资1350-1450年间翻倍。政府反扑：1349年《雇工条例》(Ordinance of Labourers)、1351年《劳工法令》(Statute of Labourers)试图把工资冻结在1346年水平、禁止工人随意流动。判决句：'立法改变不了基本算术'——人少地多，工资在罚单的缝隙里继续上涨。
租金货币化(commutation)取代劳役；继承制度松动(所有子女均可继承，不再仅限长子)；农奴制(serfdom)在1400年左右实际消亡。深远证据：1381年英格兰农民起义(Peasants' Revolt，瓦特·泰勒起义)，诉求包括废除农奴制、降低地租。
流行说法：'黑死病整村被抹去'。个案证据：1350-1500年间英格兰有超过1300个村庄被彻底废弃(deserted medieval villages)。
大样本研究(废弃村庄考古)：废弃主因是15世纪的羊毛经济(enclosure movement，圈地运动)而非黑死病。定性：一击摧毁罕见，长衰退(prolonged decline)常见。真相更复杂也更有趣。
艾希威尔(Ashwell，赫特福德郡)圣玛丽教堂石塔刻字(约1350年)：拉丁文'1349年，瘟疫惨痛暴烈，只剩穷人作为见证。'作者不可考，但这是罕见的无名者直接声音。定性：'不想让发生的事被遗忘。'
黑死病并未终结，每5-12年复发一次：1361-62年第二波(英格兰贵族死亡约23%)、1369年、1375年、1390s、1400s……延续近400年。最后一次大暴发：1665年伦敦大瘟疫、1720年马赛瘟疫。人口恢复尺度：欧洲人口直到16世纪(约200年后)才恢复到1348年水平。
为何如此致命？部分答案：(1)无细菌学说(germ theory，直到1860s才由巴斯德提出)，人们不知道真正的病因；(2)无抗生素(1940s才发明)；(3)高人口密度与营养不良使人更易感染；(4)三种病型混合爆发(腺鼠疫+肺鼠疫+败血型)。
2022年10月《自然》(麦克马斯特大学、芝加哥大学，206份古DNA样本)：黑死病在人类基因组上留下选择痕迹。ERAP2基因附近的保护型变异：携带两份该变异者在黑死病中的存活概率约高出40%。代价：该变异今天是克罗恩病(Crohn's disease)等自身免疫疾病的风险因素。
1377年7月27日，亚得里亚海港口共和国拉古萨(今克罗地亚杜布罗夫尼克)立法：来自疫区者须隔离30天(trentino)。后延长至40天(quarantina)——英文'检疫隔离'(quarantine)一词由此而来。1423年威尼斯设立世界第一个隔离检疫岛'拉萨雷托'(Lazzaretto Vecchio)。
后续大疫锚点：1665年伦敦大瘟疫(约10万人死亡)、1720年马赛瘟疫(约10万人死亡)。当代对照：抗生素时代(1940s起)鼠疫已可治疗，但至今仍有零星病例(每年全球约几百例)。
伊姆村(Eyam，德比郡，1665-1666年)：1665年夏，伦敦寄来的布料包裹把疫蚤带给裁缝乔治·维卡斯(George Viccars)，他约一周后死亡。9月底死6人，10月增至23人。教区长威廉·蒙佩松(William Mompesson)联合清教牧师托马斯·斯坦利(Thomas Stanley)说服全村：不外逃，全村自我隔离14个月。
伊姆村措施(1666年5月起)：各家自行埋葬死者；礼拜移到露天山谷(Cucklett Delph)分散举行；村界石(boundary stones)与'蒙佩松井'(Mompesson's Well)成为交易点——邻村把食物药品放在界石旁，村民把硬币泡在醋里消毒后留下付款。界石上的'瘟疫孔'(plague holes)至今可见。
伊姆村代价：273名死者被教堂登记簿记录，约260人死亡(全村人口350或约800，档案数字有争议)，仅约1/4村民幸存。人性细节：伊丽莎白·汉考克(Elizabeth Hancock)在1666年8月的8天内亲手埋葬了丈夫和6个孩子，自己活了下来('莱利墓园'Rileys graves今为英国国家信托保护地)；义务掘墓人马歇尔·豪(Marshall Howe)接触无数尸体却始终未感染。
结果：疫情被锁死在村内，未扩散至周边村镇。1891年史学家克赖顿(Charles Creighton)评价此举'出于好意'，今日被视为自我牺牲的典范。村内自1866年起每年8月最后一个星期日举行'瘟疫主日'(Plague Sunday)纪念。

谣言称犹太人在井中投毒。1348年9月萨伏依审判：犹太人阿吉迈(Agimet)在酷刑下'供认'投毒——刑讯供词被各城传抄。时间线：1349年1月9日巴塞尔全社区被烧死、1349年2月14日斯特拉斯堡约2000名犹太人被烧死(当时瘟疫尚未传到)。规模：到1351年，约350起反犹屠杀，60个大社区、150个小社区被摧毁。教皇克雷芒六世1348年7月6日与9月26日两次发布诏书明确指出'瘟疫同样降临在犹太人头上'，但地方仇恨压过了他的声音。
伊姆村教区长威廉·蒙佩松(William Mompesson)在说服全村自我隔离前，先把自己的两个孩子送去了谢菲尔德(Sheffield)避险。他的妻子凯瑟琳·蒙佩松(Catherine Mompesson)选择留下陪伴丈夫，死于1666年8月25日疫情尾声。
教皇克雷芒六世(Pope Clement VI)在阿维尼翁采取的应对措施：(1)祝圣整条罗讷河作为安葬水域(墓地不够用)；(2)宣布凡死于瘟疫者一律赦罪(因来不及做临终圣事)；(3)1348年一年他失去了6位枢机主教(Cardinals)。
威尼斯1348年成立防疫委员会(Health Board)，规范尸体转运、墓穴深度标准、禁止曝尸街头。这是欧洲最早的系统性公共卫生应对机制之一。
1361-62年第二波疫情(被称为'儿童瘟疫'pestis puerorum)显示出与首波不同的选择性：英格兰贵族死亡率约23%，儿童与青少年死亡率更高——这是因为首波幸存者已有一定免疫力，而1348年后出生的儿童从未接触过病原体。
经济史学家罗杰斯(Thorold Rogers)研究显示：15世纪英格兰雇工的实际工资水平(purchasing power)比1346年前高出约一倍，这一水平在英国直到19世纪末(约1880s-1890s)才被再次达到。
薄伽丘《十日谈》记载：他亲眼看到两头猪拱过一个死于瘟疫的穷人丢弃的破衣，猪当场打转、倒地，不久后死亡。这一细节虽无法验证，但反映了当时人对传染性的直观认知。
薄伽丘记载：瘟疫期间出现了专职收尸人(becchini)这一新行当，他们用板车或担架收集尸体、运往墓地。这些人通常来自社会底层，因高风险工作获得报酬。薄伽丘评价：'对死者的尊重，还不如今天人们对死山羊的尊重。'
波兰国王卡齐米日三世(Casimir III，又称卡齐米日大帝)在黑死病期间收留并庇护大量犹太难民，这是此后数百年东欧(特别是波兰-立陶宛联邦)成为犹太社区中心的历史起点。
1348-49年，鞭笞派(Flagellants)运动兴起：数百人规模的队伍赤裸上身、以铁刺皮鞭自笞游行赎罪，每日三次仪式、33.5天为一期(象征耶稣生命年数)。后演变为反教士运动并参与迫害犹太人，1349年10月被教皇克雷芒六世下令取缔。
黑死病期间，黑猫被当作巫术象征遭到大规模捕杀。讽刺的是，猫的减少反而助长了老鼠繁殖，可能加剧了鼠疫传播(如果鼠蚤是主要传播途径)。
2022年《自然·生态与演化》(Nature Ecology & Evolution)花粉大数据研究显示：黑死病对各地森林恢复的影响极不均衡。爱尔兰、伊比利亚半岛与东欧部分地区'侥幸过关'(受创较轻)，而英格兰、法国北部、意大利北部等地区人口锐减导致耕地大量荒废、森林局部恢复。
伊姆村自1866年起每年8月最后一个星期日举行'瘟疫主日'(Plague Sunday)纪念活动，在卡克莱特洼地(Cucklett Delph，当年露天礼拜地点)举行露天礼拜，纪念1665-1666年自我隔离期间死去的273名村民。
根据世界卫生组织(WHO)数据，鼠疫至今仍在自然界存在，每年全球仍有数百至数千例鼠疫病例报告，主要分布在非洲(刚果民主共和国、马达加斯加)、亚洲(中国、蒙古)和美洲(秘鲁、美国西部)。抗生素时代(1940s起)鼠疫已可治疗，但若不及时治疗仍可致命。

Part of the answer: no germ theory. People did not know bacteria existed until the 1860s. No antibiotics — those were not invented until the 1940s. High population density. Malnutrition. Three forms of plague attacking at once.

There is also evidence of biological selection. A 2022 *Nature* study analyzed 206 ancient DNA samples. It found that people carrying two copies of a protective variant near the ERAP2 gene had roughly 40 percent higher survival rates during the Black Death.

The plague also left institutional legacies. On July 27, 1377, the port republic of Ragusa — now Dubrovnik, Croatia — passed a law requiring travelers from plague zones to isolate for 30 days, later extended to 40. versions.text:
# Optimized Script

[CH01 | 0:00-1:37 | scene_entry]

Messina, southern Italy. Summer of 1348.

Twelve Genoese galleys arrive in port. The sailors are sick. Some have already died.

The chronicler writes: they brought "something else."

A year later, the disease reaches England. Melcombe, Dorset. Ships from Brittany dock.

In two years, it travels from Caffa on the Black Sea to the English countryside — across 2,000 miles of trade routes.

This is not one exceptional village. This is the kind of village most people lived in. England had 8,000 to 9,000 villages and manors. About 90 percent of the population — roughly five to six million people — lived in agricultural communities like this one. The same baptismal font. The same weddings. The same graveyard.

When the plague arrived, it arrived here.

---

[CH02 | 1:37-2:50 | premise_hook]

What happened next is documented history, not folklore.

The evidence: manorial court rolls listing deaths, land transfers, heriot payments. Bishops' registers tracking clergy deaths and replacements. Chronicles written by people who were there. Archaeology. Parish records.

In 2011, scientists at McMaster University and the University of Tübingen extracted DNA from teeth of plague victims buried in East Smithfield, London. They reconstructed the full genome of *Yersinia pestis*, the bacterium that caused the Black Death. That strain is the ancestor of every plague strain on earth today.

So: when the Black Death reached an English village, what actually happened?

Who had a chance to survive? How did people respond? What determined who lived and who died? What did the world look like afterward?

---

[CH03 | 2:50-5:34 | world_before_context]

Before the plague, England's population was about five to six million. Arable land had reached its limit.

The country had already been through trauma. Between 1315 and 1322, a great famine killed hundreds of thousands. In 1319, a cattle plague wiped out livestock across the country.

Most people lived under the manorial system. Peasants farmed plots on a manor. In exchange, they worked the lord's fields — plowing, harvesting, hauling grain. A week might require three days of labor for the lord, then three for the family plot. Rent came in the form of labor, not cash.

The manor court kept records of disputes, land transfers, marriages. When a tenant died, the family owed the lord a heriot — the best ox, cow, or horse the family owned. Sometimes cash instead. It was a death tax, and it was recorded every time. That's how we can count the dead today. A mundane accounting system became the archive that lets historians calculate mortality village by village.

Religion structured everything. A good death required the last rites: confession, communion, and extreme unction — anointing with holy oil. Without them, the soul could not enter heaven. The body mattered less than the soul. So when someone was dying, the priest had to come to the house.

---

[CH04 | 5:34-8:36 | knowledge_contrast]

People knew the plague was coming. News traveled along the same routes as the disease — from Caffa to Messina to England.

In 1348, the University of Paris Medical Faculty issued an explanation: an alignment of Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars had caused corrupt air — miasma — to spread disease.

The Church offered another explanation: divine punishment for human sin.

Both explanations coexisted. People accepted both.

Today's research reveals another explanation.

In 2011, researchers confirmed the pathogen: *Yersinia pestis*. In 2022, a team from the Max Planck Institute traced its origin to Central Asia, near Lake Issyk-Kul in present-day Kyrgyzstan. Tombstones from 1338–1339 record "pestilence." DNA extracted from three bodies confirmed plague bacteria.

The transmission mechanism is still debated. The mainstream view: rat fleas spread bubonic plague. But the Black Death moved faster than rat-flea transmission alone can explain. Human fleas and lice may have played a role. Scientists are still working on it.

But people in 1348 could only see what the disease did. Swellings in the groin and armpits. Black spots spreading across the skin. Death.

---

[CH05 | 8:36-10:17 | arrival_mechanism]

The plague spread along existing networks. Markets met once a week. Mills ground grain for multiple households. Churches held Sunday services. Manor courts settled disputes. People traveled short distances constantly. To the next village. To the nearest town.

Some cities tried to stop it. They closed gates. They banned travelers from infected areas.

It didn't work.

The disease had already entered before the gates closed. Merchants kept moving. Pilgrims kept traveling. Armies marched. Rats and fleas ignored human borders.

Boccaccio put it simply: the plague came "like any other goods, by the roads."

So the plague reached villages the same way everything else did. By road.

---

[CH06 | 10:17-12:05 | stakes_immersion]

A typical peasant house: timber frame, wattle-and-daub walls, thatched roof. Grain stored indoors in sacks or barrels.

Warm. Dark. Food everywhere. The structure was comfortable for rats and fleas too.

When the plague arrived, this is what people saw.

Boccaccio described it: swellings the size of eggs or apples appeared in the groin or armpit. Then black spots spread across the body. Those spots were a death sentence.

He also recorded this: he saw two pigs rooting through rags discarded by a plague victim. The pigs staggered, collapsed, and died shortly after.

There were three forms of plague. Bubonic plague — transmitted by flea bites — caused swollen lymph nodes and killed 50 to 60 percent of victims without treatment. Pneumonic plague — airborne, human-to-human — caused coughing and bloody sputum. It killed nearly everyone within three days. Septicemic plague — bacteria directly in the bloodstream — could kill within 24 hours.

---

[CH07 | 12:05-13:45 | care_system]

Manorial records show no payments to physicians. Hospitals, where they existed, served cities and monasteries. Physicians were rare and expensive. Ordinary villagers could not afford them.

Care fell to families and neighbors.

A new occupation emerged: *becchini*, professional corpse collectors. They came from the poorest layers of society and were paid to haul bodies on carts or stretchers.

Guy de Chauliac, the pope's physician, recommended burning fires day and night in the sickroom, refusing visitors, and avoiding bad air. Pope Clement VI followed the advice and survived.

The measures helped. Fire and isolation reduced exposure to airborne and contact transmission. But they could not stop flea-borne spread.

The pope also took other steps. He consecrated the entire Rhône River as a burial site when graveyards ran out of space. He declared that anyone who died of plague would be absolved of sin, since there was no time for last rites. In 1348 alone, he lost six cardinals.

Priests went house to house to administer last rites: confession, communion, anointing. They had to enter the rooms where the sick were dying. They had to touch them.

That made clergy the most exposed group.

---

[CH08 | 13:45-15:42 | institutional_strain]

Bishops' registers show the toll. Approximately four out of every ten parish clergy with a benefice died during the epidemic. Some parishes replaced the priest twice in a single year.

The system bent under pressure.

Ralph of Shrewsbury, Bishop of Bath and Wells, issued a written document around 1348. It stated: a person facing death without access to a priest could confess to a layperson. If no man was available, even to a woman.

This is the most astonishing document in the entire story.

It is a written adjustment to the most important sacrament in medieval Christianity. It shows how far the institution had to bend to keep functioning.

---

[CH09 | 15:42-18:33 | dignity_reveal]

Normally, the dead were buried in the churchyard. A priest presided. The family attended.

When death rates spiked, the system strained. Pope Clement consecrated the Rhône River as burial space. Venice established a health board in 1348 to regulate corpse transport and mandate grave depth.

Archaeologists excavated a mass grave in East Smithfield, London — used between 1348 and 1350. It held 48 bodies. More than half were children. But they were still laid out head-to-foot in organized rows.

What struck researchers was not chaos. It was order.

Even under extreme pressure, the people who buried them tried to maintain dignity.

Boccaccio described people fleeing, abandoning the sick. But archaeology and records show that most people stayed. They cared for the sick. They buried the dead. They kept the system running.

The clearest example: Eyam, a village in Derbyshire. In 1665, plague arrived in a cloth shipment from London. The tailor who received it, George Viccars, died within a week. By September, six were dead. By October, 23.

The rector, William Mompesson, and the Puritan minister Thomas Stanley convinced the village to seal itself off. No one would leave for 14 months.

They moved church services outdoors to a valley called Cucklett Delph. Families buried their own dead. Neighboring villages left food and medicine at boundary stones. Villagers paid with coins soaked in vinegar.

Elizabeth Hancock buried her husband and six children in eight days in August 1666. She survived. Marshall Howe, the gravedigger, handled countless bodies and never got sick.

273 people died — about 260 recorded deaths out of a population estimated between 350 and 800. Roughly one in four survived.

The plague stayed contained. It did not spread to surrounding villages.

The village has held a memorial service every August since 1866.

So before we go further: if you want to see how this story ends, subscribe now. The most surprising part happens after the dying stops.

---

[CH10 | 18:33-21:35 | death_accounting]

Now: how do we know how many people died?

Because of heriot.

When a tenant died, the manor court recorded the payment. One ox. One cow. Sometimes cash. Every death generated a record.

Historians studying these court rolls have calculated mortality rates village by village.

Halesowen manor: 40 to 43 percent of tenants died. Winchester episcopal estates: close to 50 percent. Cottenham in Cambridgeshire: 49 percent.

The most shocking case: an Essex manor where all twelve principal tenant farmers — peasants who held standard family farms — died in 1349. In a single season.

These were not marginal figures. They were the backbone of the village. They plowed the most land. They owed the most labor. They testified in court. They organized the harvest.

Now their names stopped appearing in the records.

Overall, English villages lost between one-third and one-half of their population — some regions as high as 60 percent. Some areas lost 60 percent. But the variation was enormous. Some villages lost only 10 to 20 percent. Others nearly vanished.

---

[CH11 | 21:35-23:13 | aftermath_tableau]

Harvest season does not wait. Neither does planting season.

Agnolo di Tura, a chronicler in Siena, wrote: "I buried my five children with my own hands. Many said and believed: this is the end of the world."

English chronicles recorded: "Fields went unharvested. Houses stood empty."

Fields. Houses. Villages. Mills.

The land did not change. But the people who worked it were gone.

Before, a peasant might wait his entire life to inherit his father's land. Now he could choose between multiple manors.

Neighboring lords were competing for labor. They offered lower rents. Fewer labor obligations.

Economic historian Thorold Rogers calculated that real wages in 15th-century England were about double what they had been before 1346. That level was not reached again until the 1880s or 1890s — roughly 500 years later.

---

[CH12 | 23:13-25:39 | consequence_chain]

Survivors realized they had bargaining power.

Lords needed labor. Survivors could walk to the next village and negotiate better terms.

The government tried to suppress it. In 1349, Parliament passed the Ordinance of Labourers. In 1351, the Statute of Labourers. Both laws attempted to freeze wages at 1346 levels and prohibit workers from moving freely.

Basic arithmetic could not be overridden. There were far fewer people, but just as much land.

Wages rose anyway, through the cracks in enforcement.

Over the next decades, the system transformed. Rent payments shifted from labor to cash. Inheritance rules loosened — younger sons and daughters could inherit, not just the eldest son. Serfdom effectively disappeared by around 1400.

The long-term evidence: the Peasants' Revolt of 1381. Tens of thousands marched on London demanding the abolition of serfdom and lower rents.

---

[CH13 | 25:39-26:50 | myth_correction]

Popular belief holds that the Black Death wiped out entire villages overnight.

There is evidence for it. Between 1350 and 1500, more than 1,300 English villages were abandoned.

The reality is more complicated.

Large-scale studies of deserted villages show that most were abandoned in the 15th century due to the wool economy and enclosure, not the Black Death.

Instant destruction was rare. Prolonged decline was common.

---

[CH14 | 26:50-28:41 | survivor_voice]

Direct testimony from ordinary people is rare.

But there is one.

In the church tower of St. Mary's, Ashwell, Hertfordshire, someone carved an inscription around 1350. In Latin: "1349. The plague was fierce and violent. Only the poor remain to witness."

We do not know who wrote it.

An anonymous witness carved a warning for future generations.

The plague did not end in 1349.

It returned in 1361–62. Then 1369. Then 1375. Then the 1390s. Then the 1400s. It came back every five to twelve years for nearly 400 years.

The second wave in 1361–62 showed different selectivity. English nobles died at about 23 percent — lower than the first wave. But children and teenagers died at higher rates. Survivors of the first wave had some immunity. Children born after 1348 had none.

Europe's population did not recover to 1348 levels until the 16th century — roughly 200 years later.

---

[CH15 | 28:41-30:49 | legacy_bridge]

So why was it so deadly?

Part of the answer: no germ theory. People did not know bacteria existed until the 1860s. No antibiotics — those were not invented until the 1940s. High population density. Malnutrition. Three forms of plague attacking at once.

There is also evidence of biological selection. A 2022 *Nature* study analyzed 206 ancient DNA samples. It found that people carrying two copies of a protective variant near the ERAP2 gene had roughly 40 percent higher survival rates during the Black Death.

The cost: that same variant is a risk factor for Crohn's disease and other autoimmune disorders today.

The plague also left institutional legacies. On July 27, 1377, the port republic of Ragusa — now Dubrovnik, Croatia — passed a law requiring travelers from plague zones to isolate for 30 days, later extended to 40. The English word "quarantine" comes from the Italian *quarantina* — forty days. In 1423, Venice established the world's first quarantine island, Lazzaretto Vecchio.

The plague returned in 1665 in London — roughly 100,000 dead. In 1720 in Marseille — again, around 100,000.

Today, antibiotics can treat plague if caught early. But it has not disappeared. According to the World Health Organization, there are still several hundred to several thousand cases globally each year, mainly in Africa, Asia, and the Americas.

One more thing. In 1348, there were no plague doctors in bird masks. That costume was invented in 1619. The nursery rhyme "Ring Around the Rosie" is not about the Black Death — that is a later myth. The claim that Jews were immune or poisoned wells? Pope Clement VI pointed out at the time that Jews were dying in large numbers too. Between 1348 and 1351, about 350 anti-Jewish massacres occurred, 60 large communities and 150 small ones were destroyed.

---

[CH16 | 30:49-33:05 | closure]

So: when the Black Death reached an English village, what happened?

How did it arrive? Along trade routes and everyday networks. Markets. Mills. Churches. Courts. It came the same way everything else came.

How many died? Between one-third and one-half. In some places, 60 percent. In one Essex manor, all twelve principal tenant farmers died in the same season.

Why was it so deadly? No knowledge of bacteria. No antibiotics. Malnutrition. Genetic variation. Three forms of plague at once. How exactly it spread — rat fleas, human lice, or both — remains debated.

What changed? Labor became scarce. Wages doubled. Serfdom collapsed. Parliament tried to freeze wages. Basic arithmetic defeated the law. Rent shifted from labor to cash. Inheritance rules loosened. In 1381, tens of thousands of peasants marched on London.

The village did not end. In most places, it continued.

Someone plowed the field. Someone rang the church bell. Someone recorded the heriot payment in the court roll.

Forests began to recover in some regions — pollen data from 2022 shows that farmland reverted to woodland in England, northern France, and northern Italy, though Ireland and parts of Eastern Europe were less affected.

At Eyam, survivors kept living. The village has held a memorial service every year since 1866. The author of the Ashwell inscription is lost to history.

The plague came back every five to twelve years for nearly 400 years. It did not truly end until the age of antibiotics. Even today, the World Health Organization records hundreds to thousands of cases annually.

The most amazing thing is not the death toll. It is that they continued.

We think of plague as distant history. But it returned for four centuries. Only antibiotics made it truly treatable.

Chronicled at the scale of kingdoms and continents. Lived at the scale of cottages and fields.
